meta.title: How Does Fox News Frame the WNBA?
meta.description: Analyzing the right-wing politicization of the Women’s National Basketball Association
meta.hed: How Does Fox News Frame the WNBA?
meta.dek: Analyzing the right-wing politicization of the Women’s National Basketball Association
meta.headerImg: wnba-framed.png | The WNBA logo hung inside an empty gilt picture frame

content.value: Though I have loved (and played) basketball most of my life, I finally became a real WNBA fan when I moved to Seattle five years ago. (Let’s go, Storm.) Since then, I have also become fixated on a question. Why is Fox News obsessed with the WNBA?

fox-iran-wnba.png | Fox News homepage navigation listing its Hot Topics: War With Iran, then WNBA Controversy | A screenshot from the Fox News home page in August 2026. Their hottest topics: literal war and women’s basketball.
This question dawned on me slowly, especially since I don’t read or watch Fox News myself.

The first clue: my web browser. As I started reading more WNBA news, my Google Chrome app recommended more WNBA news. That made sense. But then I started getting served coverage from, of all places, Fox News.
Wait, what?
It wasn’t just one article, either. I saw dozens of Fox News takes on women’s basketball, often with a clear political bias, and an implicitly racist and homophobic framing.
Caitlin Clark, Alyssa Thomas, DiJonai Carrington, Angel Reese

Headline after headline pit the league’s most famous straight white star, Caitlin Clark, against other WNBA players, mainly Black and/or queer women, like Alyssa Thomas, DiJonai Carrington, or Angel Reese.

content.value: Why does Fox News talk about Carrington, Cloud, and Griner so much?
DiJonai Carrington, Natasha Cloud, Brittney Griner

It’s political. These players’ vocal leftist views—on race, gender, BLM and more—make them a target for conservative coverage of the WNBA, which has long sought to frame the league as both dangerously radical and illegitimate. (It’s no coincidence that these are all queer Black women, too.)

For example, Carrington has publicly criticized Clark for not being vocal enough in denouncing her racist and bigoted fans. She has fouled Clark and Cunningham in high-profile ways. And she doesn’t like Trump.

content.value: Cloud’s outspoken activism—for Black Lives Matter, for Gaza—has also been a focal point. And Griner was the subject of consistent conversation when she was imprisoned in Russia in 2022, though she is often criticized for her progressive views, too.
I knew the WNBA was being talked about on Fox News TV programs, too.

At a holiday gathering, I was chatting with an older conservative family member, who, out of the blue, started name-dropping WNBA players, saying praiseworthy things about Clark and suspect things about other Black players.
This person has never seen a WNBA game in their life. But they do mainline Fox News on cable TV.

steps.text: Sure enough, Fox News talks more about Clark ((Caitlin Clark| face)) and Cunningham ((Sophie Cunningham| face)) on TV, too.
This is cable news coverage of the WNBA, via their chyrons—you know, those headlines that appear at the bottom of your screen.
Fox News talks incessantly about fouls against Clark.
They also talk way more about trans women in sports.
Especially recently.
Search any term.

content.value: In the summer of 2026, the right-wing politicization of the WNBA burst into the mainstream.

In July, Sophie Cunningham ((Sophie Cunningham|face)), the Fever’s shooting guard, made openly anti-trans remarks. This inspired right-wing politicians and anti-trans advocates around the world to rally around her, including Vice President J.D. Vance and infamous TERF J.K. Rowling.
vance-cunningham-fox.png | Fox News segment showing Vice President J.D. Vance praising Sophie Cunningham | Vice President J.D. Vance praises Sophie Cunningham on Fox News, August 2026.

Even Fox News political pundits are confused and exhausted by the WNBA coverage. As commentator Jesse Watters recently said on air: “We have to do this again, really? Someone wore a t-shirt at a WNBA game? This isn’t a news story…. We don’t even cover the NBA. Why are we covering the WNBA?”
https://www.youtube.com/shorts/k1aa6ip2HA4
How did professional women’s basketball—a league that, for decades, most people didn’t watch or care anything about—transform into a mainstream political lightning rod?
It didn’t happen overnight. And the media, especially conservative media, played a key role.
So let’s dive into how Fox News has framed the WNBA as a hot-button culture war issue—one that was primed, at the right moment, to explode.
The Data
To explore how conservative media frames the WNBA, I collected any Fox News article that mentioned the WNBA or its players over the past six years.
This includes coverage from Outkick, now owned by Fox. It touts itself as “the antidote to the mainstream sports media that often serves an elite, left-leaning minority.”

value.caption: Every article has a headline; full text where the outlet allows it. The Athletic is paywalled, so it is headlines only. Counts run through Aug 2026.

content.value: As a comparison, I collected parallel WNBA coverage from ESPN, USA Today, CBS Sports, The Athletic (owned by the New York Times), and Just Women’s Sports.

Additionally, I gathered nine years worth of cable news chyrons from Fox, MSNBC, and CNN, drawing on data from the Internet Archive's Third Eye OCR feed, and inspired by a very cool analysis by Charlie Smart.
The Timeline
Let’s look at the broad timeline.
For most of its history, Fox News barely covered the WNBA. They talked about the NBA much more.

value.caption: Mentions of Caitlin Clark in Fox WNBA articles

content.value: But you can see that coverage clearly surges in the “Caitlin Clark era”—that is, after Clark was drafted into the league in April 2024.
However, Fox News has always put a conservative—and I would say misogynistic, racist, and homophic—spin on their WNBA coverage One way they’ve achieved this is through a reliable cast of characters.
The Fox News-WNBA Expanded Universe
Fox News often speaks the most loudly through the voices they platform, using them as mouthpieces for views they want to express but don’t want to be blamed for.
What’s more, Fox pits players against each other in ways that amplify divisive political narratives, especially in click-bait headlines.
Let’s look at the web they’ve been spinning.

content.value: “Identity Politics”
Fox News is obsessed with rejecting ”identity politics” in WNBA coverage. Recently, Bobby Burack criticized ESPN for being “racial idolaters” in reporting about Clark:

From day one, the narrative around Clark is that she is a superstar only because America has starved for a straight white girl to save them from a league of largely black LGBTQ women. That narrative is not supported by the history of superstardom in American sports. Yet it has shaped ESPN's coverage from the start… ESPN ought to add some diversity to its WNBA commentary—diversity of opinion, that is.
Here’s the irony, though. Fox News talks about race, gender, and identity politics more than any other outlet, including ESPN.

content.value: Across all the outlets, discussion of race, racial justice, and the WNBA peaks in 2020, the height of the Black Lives Matter movement. This is true for Fox, too.

wnba-blm-2020.jpg | Minnesota Lynx players standing with linked arms, wearing “Say Her Name” shirts | Minnesota Lynx players wear “Say Her Name” shirts and lock arms during a moment of silence in honor of Breonna Taylor before a game in July 2020. Phelan M. Ebenhack/AP

In 2020, WNBA players engaged in highly visible protest in support of the Black Lives Matter movement. They walked off the court during the national anthem, wore BLM and “Say Her Name” shirts on national television, and successfully campaigned to unseat a team owner who sat in the U.S. Senate, Kelly Loeffler, after she opposed players’ activism.
This was frequently covered by Fox, and often framed in implicitly disapproving terms.
the protests | July 2020 | green | Sen. Kelly Loeffler, co-owner of Atlanta Dream, ==objects to WNBA's social justice plans==
the protests | July 2020 | green | WNBA players call on league to ==stop playing national anthem==
Increasingly, they also spotlighted the league’s LGBTQ+ players and related issues, including trans women’s participation in sports.

Enter Caitlin Clark
Things changed when, in 2024, Clark, the three-point phenom from Iowa, was drafted #1 in the WNBA.

clark-fever-spurlock.jpg | Caitlin Clark, seen from behind in her white Indiana Fever number 22 jersey, releases a jump shot toward the basket. | Photo by Brian Spurlock/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images
Clark’s popularity drew millions of new viewers and fans to the league. But it has also launched the WNBA into a culture war debate.

Many commentators have noted that Clark’s background as a straight, white, Midwestern star may play a role in her broad appeal. It is undeniable that Clark has drawn in a whiter, more conservative, and more mainstream audience than the WNBA—a historically Black and queer league—has had in the past.
why-does-left-hate-clark-fox.png
everything's-racist-fox
Fox News has been obsessed with dispelling the identity-related dimension of this narrative.

At the same time, Fox News has played up Clark’s treatment in the league, specifically hard fouls committed against her, often in implicitly racialized terms that malign the Black and/or queer players who committed the fouls.

steps.text: Case in point: Fox News has consistently discussed “hard” fouls against Caitlin Clark more than other outlets.

steps.words: race, racism, racist, privilege, black, white
steps.text: They also invoked race and racism more than other outlets, as well as culture war buzzwords like “privilege.”

This is especially true because trolls “will just use this controversy to denigrate the rest of the WNBA. “No amount of good PR,” she warns, “is going to stop clickbait or the right’s obsession with criticizing the WNBA.”

content.value: Who Gets Framed How?
Trans Women in Sports

Fox News consistently fanned the flames of the WNBA culture war. They denied that race, sexuality, or gender were relevant considerations in the league, yet foregrounded them more than any other outlet.

The implicit misogyny, and suspicion of “social justice” and queer communities, laid the groundwork for the right-wing, anti-trans movement to rise up and seize the WNBA as a central issue—even though no trans women currently even play in the league.

value.title: Fox WNBA articles about trans athletes
value.caption: Fox WNBA articles per month that mention trans athletes or eligibility in women’s sports. Source: Fox News.

steps.text: Through 2025, Fox planted the seed for controversy around trans issues and the WNBA, discussing it periodically but consistently.
Then, in 2026, it exploded.
And as a share of everything Fox writes about the WNBA, trans coverage went from a sliver to the majority: in August 2026, nearly two out of every three Fox WNBA articles mention trans athletes.

content.value: Among the TV networks, Fox News talks about trans issues way more than the others.

As Jesse Watters recently said on air, “Why are we covering the WNBA?” Or, more pointedly, “This is something I don’t care about.” Watters said the quiet part out loud. Fox News doesn’t actually care about women’s basketball. Right-wing pundits and politicians are using the WNBA to push their own agenda.

Sports are political. They have always been political. Throughout American history, athletes have been able to use their platform to advocate for justice. Players in the WNBA are a great example. But we should be wary of how narratives about the WNBA are being framed by the right-wing media and outside parties who have little to no actual investment in the league.

When I went to my first WNBA game, I was shocked by how inclusive it felt. It was completely different from every other (men’s) professional sporting event I had ever been to. The version of the WNBA presented by Fox News is not recognizable to me. We need to recognize this framing—and push back against it—lest we all get played.
Data and Methods
I collected WNBA articles from Fox News, ESPN, Yahoo Sports, Just Women’s Sports, The Athletic, CBS Sports, and USA Today.
The chyrons come from the Internet Archive’s Third Eye project.
The word comparisons use “fightin’ words” aka weighted log-odds with an informative Dirichlet prior (Monroe, Colaresi & Quinn 2008).
You can find data and code on GitHub.
